argument: Nietzsche's amor fati calls for affirming rather than negating one's own desires and fate, as an alternative to the rational-pessimistic strategy of treating desire as an enemy to be renounced. Affirmation is a psychological shift, not a rule to say yes to everything: you can affirm a desire as genuinely part of you while still not acting on it. Because affirming life honestly means affirming things as they truly are, this creates a built-in commitment to truth, but Nietzsche also values art and moral pluralism over monism, since any single value pushed to an extreme starts to undermine itself and the other values it's connected to.
keyIdeas: Nietzsche never offers a detailed prescription for which values to hold; the more finished and detailed a picture someone is trying to sell you of how to live, the more skepticism you should bring to it.

Following Schopenhauer's rational pessimism, actually getting what you want can't produce lasting happiness, because satisfaction is temporary: the new state of affairs quickly becomes normal and a fresh desire takes its place. Traditional asceticism responds to this with an 'attitude of negation,' treating some desires as evil parts of the self to be silenced or punished.

Amor fati is a psychological shift in how you relate to necessity and suffering, not necessarily a change in what you do; you can affirm a short-term desire as genuinely your own while still choosing not to act on it.

Because affirming life honestly means affirming things as they actually are, committing to amor fati creates an almost built-in commitment to truth; but Nietzsche also values art, since illusions and appearances are an undeniable part of existence, and art and truth counterbalance each other.

Nietzsche favors moral pluralism over monism: maximizing any single value without limit, like honesty, can undermine other things a person cares about, so values should be treated as interconnected rather than subordinated to one supreme value.
